title: How to Spot a Scholarship That Is Actually Worth Your Time
excerpt: The skill is not writing better essays. It is filtering ruthlessly, so your effort lands where it can win.
content:
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from applying for scholarships. You spend three weekends on an application, you write an essay about your dreams, you chase two referees, and then you hear nothing. Ever. Not a rejection, just silence. Do that four or five times and most people quietly decide the whole thing is rigged.

It usually is not rigged. What normally happened is that the application was never going to succeed, and it was possible to know that before starting. The skill worth building is not writing better essays. It is filtering ruthlessly, so your effort lands where it can actually win.

First, check that it is real

A depressing share of what circulates on WhatsApp is not a scholarship at all. Some are outright scams. Others are marketing for an agency that will charge you for services you do not need. A few are real programmes that closed three years ago and never stopped being forwarded.

Three checks, none of which take longer than five minutes:

  • Find it on the institution’s own website. Not a blog, not an aggregator, not the message you were sent. The university or foundation itself. If it does not exist there, it does not exist.
  • Check whether money flows the wrong way. Legitimate scholarships do not charge an application fee to consider you. Visa fees and exam fees paid directly to governments and test providers are normal. A fee paid to the scholarship itself is not.
  • Look at the deadline against the calendar. Recycled posts are everywhere. Confirm this year’s cycle is genuinely open.

Then check what it actually covers

This is where people get hurt, and it is entirely avoidable. The word scholarship covers everything from a small contribution to a package that pays for your whole life abroad. They are not the same opportunity, and accepting the wrong one can leave you stranded.

Work out precisely which of these you are being offered:

  • Tuition only. Very common. You still need to fund rent, food, flights, visa and insurance yourself.
  • Tuition plus stipend. Much stronger. Check the stipend against the actual cost of living in that city, not the national average.
  • Fully funded. Tuition, living costs, and usually flights. These are rare and fiercely competitive.
  • Partial or percentage award. A 30 percent tuition reduction is useful, but it is a discount, not a scholarship in the sense most people mean.

Then do the honest arithmetic. Write down the total annual cost, subtract what the award covers, and look hard at the number left over. If you cannot fund that gap without borrowing at rates that will follow you for a decade, this opportunity is not for you this year, no matter how prestigious the name attached to it.

Read the eligibility criteria as a filter, not a suggestion

Hard requirements are hard. If it says two years of full time work experience, and you have fourteen months, you are not a borderline case being brave. You are an automatic rejection that a human being will never read.

The distinction worth learning is between requirements and preferences. Must hold a first degree in engineering is a wall. Preference given to candidates with community leadership experience is a door left slightly open. Spend your energy on applications where you clear every wall and can argue well on the preferences.

Estimate your real odds

Some scholarships publish how many awards they give and how many people apply. Many do not, but you can usually find rough figures in past coverage or alumni interviews.

This is not to talk you out of ambitious applications. Apply for the famous ones. But know the difference between the programme taking 40 people out of 60,000 and the departmental award at a good but less glamorous university taking 15 out of 300. The second one is not a lesser life. It is frequently the one that actually changes it, and almost nobody forwards it on WhatsApp.

A simple system

Keep a single sheet. One row per opportunity, with columns for the deadline, what it funds, the gap you would need to cover, whether you meet every hard requirement, and the link to the official page.

Fill it in as you find things, and only start writing once a row survives every column. Most will not. That is the point. The sheet is doing the painful work of saying no, so that your weekends go to the three applications where you are genuinely competitive rather than the twelve where you were never in the running.

Fewer applications, better targeted, done properly. That is the whole strategy, and it beats volume every time.
author: Fisayo Adeyemi
